verses.zh: 当犹大王乌西雅，以色列王约阿施的儿子耶罗波安在位的时候，大地震前二年，提哥亚牧人中的阿摩司得默示论以色列。
verses.en: The following is a record of what Amos prophesied.[NOTE:1] He[NOTE:2] was one of the herdsmen from Tekoa. These prophecies about Israel were revealed to him[NOTE:3] during the time of[NOTE:4] King Uzziah of Judah and[NOTE:5] King Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel, two years before the earthquake.[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “The words of Amos.” Among the prophetic books this opening phrase finds a parallel only at Jer 1:1 but is not that uncommon in other genres (note, e.g., Prov 30:1; 31:1; Eccl 1:1; Neh 1:1).
Heb “who.” Here a new sentence has been started in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “which he saw concerning Israel.”
Heb “in the days of.”
The Hebrew text repeats, “and in the days of.” This phrase has not been repeated in the translation for stylistic reasons.

This refers to a well-known earthquake that occurred during the first half of the 8th century b.c. According to a generally accepted dating system, Uzziah was a co-regent with his father Amaziah from 792-767 b.c. and ruled independently from 767-740 b.c. Jeroboam II was a co-regent with his father Joash from 793-782 b.c. and ruled independently from 782-753 b.c. Since only Uzziah and Jeroboam are mentioned in the introduction it is likely that Amos’ mission to Israel and the earthquake which followed occurred between 767-753 b.c. The introduction validates the genuine character of Amos’ prophetic ministry in at least two ways. First, Amos was not a native Israelite or a prophet by trade. Rather he was a herdsman in Tekoa, located in Judah. His mere presence in the northern kingdom as a prophet was evidence that he had been called by God (see 7:14-15). Second, the mighty earthquake shortly after Amos’ ministry would have been interpreted as an omen or signal of approaching judgment. The clearest references to an earthquake are 1:1 and 9:1, 5. It is possible that the verb הָפַךְ (hafakh, “overturn”) at 3:13-15; 4:11; 6:11, and 8:8 also refers to an earthquake, as might the descriptions at 2:13 and 6:9-10. Evidence of a powerful earthquake has been correlated with a destruction layer at Hazor and other sites. Its lasting impact is evident by its mention in Zech 14:5 and 2 Chr 26:16-21. Earthquake imagery appears in later prophets as well (cf. D. N. Freedman and A. Welch, “Amos’s Earthquake and Israelite Prophecy,” Scripture and Other Artifacts, 188-98). On the other hand, some of these verses in Amos could allude to the devastation that would be caused by the imminent military invasion.
verses.commentary:
1:1 "Amos" For the supposed meanings of this rare name see Introduction, I., B.

▣ "the sheepherders" This term occurs only one other time in the OT, "sheepmaster," used
of Mesha, King of Moab (cf. 2 Kgs. 3:4). Amos' occupation could also relate to the care of cattle (BDB 133, cf. Amos 7:14).
This is an unusual term (BDB 667, KB 719-720) and could refer to the ownership of a special kind of diminutive
sheep (BDB 838, cf. Amos 7:15). Amos was

- following Jewish tradition, a well-to-do businessman (sheep breeder, cf. The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1177)

- he was a poor herdsman and itinerant agricultural worker

The Hebrew consonantal root נקד (KB 719-720) has many meanings.

- to prick, to puncture

- to clean, to shine (Arabic, "to free" or "to save")

- a poor type of sheep

- money (Talmud, a small coin)

- speckled (cf. Gen. 30:32)

- shepherd, herdsman, sheep breeder

- title for high official (Ugaritic)

Context is crucial! Only context defines words. Cognates are only helpful when the word is
rare. In Amos there are several words used to describe his occupation before his call by God.

- "shepherd," Amos 1:1 (BDB 667)

- "herdsman," Amos 7:14 (BDB 133)

- "from following the flock," Amos 7:15 (BDB 29 CONSTRUCT BDB 838)

▣ "Tekoa" The name (BDB 1075, KB 1785) means "to pitch a tent" (cf. Gen. 31:25; Jer: 6:3) or "to blow
a trumpet" (cf. Ezek. 7:14). Tekoa is a city in the Judean desert, overlooking the Judean wilderness. It was
about five miles south of Bethlehem. Isn't it amazing how many of God's leaders have come from the pastoral lifestyle?

▣ "which he envisioned in visions" The term is literally "saw" (BDB 302, KB 301, Qal
PERFECT). It is regularly used of an ecstatic vision (cf. Num. 24:4,16; Isa. 1:1; 2:1,13; Ezek. 12:27;
13:16; Micah 1:1; Hab. 1:1). It came to be one of three words used to designate a prophet (i.e. "seer," e.g. Amos 7:12;
2 Sam. 24:11; 2 Kgs. 17:13; 1 Chr. 21:9; 29:29; 2 Chr. 9:29; 12:15; 19:2; 29:25,29; 33:19; 35:15; Isa. 29:10,25; 30:10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHET (the different Hebrew terms)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣ "the days of Uzziah king of Judah" He was a godly king who reigned in Judah from 783-742 B.C. The
fact that the king of Judah was mentioned at all shows the prophet's theological orientation toward Jerusalem. The
prophets always condemn the splitting of the tribes in 922 B.C. (cf. 1 Kgs. 12:16-20; 2 Chronicles 10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

▣ "the days of Jeroboam. . .king of Israel" This refers to Jeroboam II (BDB 914), who reigned over
the Northern Ten Tribes from 786-746 B.C. He was a very successful and efficient Monarch. Both
Judah and Israel, at this period, were enjoying great prosperity because Assyria had defeated their traditional
enemy to the north, Syria. Also, Assyria and Egypt were not expansionists during this period (see Introduction, VI).

▣ "two years before the earthquake" This must have been a very strong earthquake because it is
mentioned years later in Zech. 14:5. It may be alluded to in Amos 8:8 and 9:1. Josephus (Antiq. 9.225) tells
us that it is related to Uzziah's sin of offering of a sacrifice (cf. 2 Chr. 26:16-21). This is either

- a historical statement in an attempt to precisely set the date for Amos' prophecy (Amos 1:1 is the
most extensive dating attempt of any book of the OT)

- a way of reinforcing the judgment theme of Amos' message from YHWH

See note in NET Bible, p. 1589, #6.

verses.zh: 他说：耶和华必从锡安吼叫，从耶路撒冷发声；牧人的草场要悲哀；迦密的山顶要枯干。
verses.en: Amos[NOTE:1] said:“The Lord comes roaring[NOTE:2] out of Zion;from Jerusalem[NOTE:3] he comes bellowing![NOTE:4] The shepherds’ pastures wilt;[NOTE:5] the summit of Carmel[NOTE:6] withers.”[NOTE:7]
notes: Heb “he;” the referent (Amos) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The Lord, in his role of warrior-king, is compared to a lion. See 3:4, 8.
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Heb “gives his voice.”

Lexicographers debate whether there are two roots אָבַל (ʾaval), one signifying “mourn” and the other “be dry,” or simply one (“mourn”). The parallel verb (“withers”) might favor the second option and have the meaning “wilt away.” It is interesting to note, however, that the root appears later in the book in the context of lament (5:16; 8:8, 10; 9:5). Either 1:2 is a possible wordplay to alert the reader to the death that will accompany the judgment (the option of two roots), or perhaps the translation “mourns” is appropriate here as well (cf. KJV, NASB, NKJV, NJPS; see also D. J. A. Clines, “Was There an ’BL II ‘Be Dry’ in Classical Hebrew?” VT 42 [1992]: 1-10).
Carmel was a region known for its abundant plants and trees. See Isa 33:9; 35:2; Jer 50:19.
Loss of a land’s fertility is frequently associated with judgment in the OT and ancient Near Eastern literature.
verses.commentary:
1:2 This begins the first poetic section in Amos. It is a summary of the entire book. See Introduction, VII.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

▣ "the Lord roars" The term "roars" (BDB 980, KB 1367, Qal
IMPERFECT) was also used of YHWH's voice as thunder, Job 37:3-5 and Jer. 25:30. This seems
to refer to His judgment (cf. Amos 3:8) based on Israel's sins amidst their covenantal knowledge (the nations mentioned
were all part of David and Solomon's kingdoms and, therefore, had some knowledge of YHWH). This is similar to Joel 3:16.

The roar is the climactic moment of a lion's kill, the moment of judgment. It can refer to

- deliverance, as in Joel 3:16; Hosea 11:10

- but in this context of God's judgment

The Shepherd (Psalm 23:4c) has become the aggressive attacker! What a role reversal sin causes!!

For "Lord (YHWH)" see
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "Zion. . .Jerusalem" These two names are in a synonymous, parallel relationship. The Israelites
envisioned YHWH as symbolically dwelling between the wings of the Cherubim over the Ark of the Covenant in
the Holy of Holies of the temple on Mt. Moriah in Jerusalem (cf. Exod. 25:22).

Jerusalem was built on seven hills.

- Mt. Zion was the hill on which the Jebusite citadel was located, which was not captured until
David's day (cf. Josh. 15:63; 2 Sam. 5:6-10). David built his palace on this hill.

- Mt. Moriah was the hill on which the temple was built (cf. Gen. 22:2; 1 Chr. 21:1-22; 2 Chr. 3:1).

The mention of Jerusalem as the place from which YHWH roars was a subtle way to reject
the golden calves which Jeroboam I set up at Bethel and Dan in Israel. YHWH dwelt in Judah's temple
(cf. Amos 9:11), not Israel's shrines (cf. Amos 4:4; 5:5; 8:14)!

The original etymology of both "Zion" (BDB 851, KB 1022) and "Jerusalem" (BDB 436, KB 437) is uncertain.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MORIAH, SALEM, JEBUS, ZION, JERUSALEM

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ARK OF THE COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHERUBIM

▣ "the shepherd's pasture grounds mourn, and the summit of Carmel dries up" YHWH's judgment
on mankind's sin affects nature (cf. Genesis 3; Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28; Romans 8:18-25; and the seals
and bowls judgments of the book of Revelation). God uses nature to get mankind's attention (e.g. Amos 1:1c; 4:6-13; Ps. 19:1-6).

▣ "Carmel" Carmel was a mountain range in northern Israel that runs into the Mediterranean. It's
name meant "vineyard of God" (BDB 501). It was proverbial for its lush vegetation (BDB 502) because it received so much annual rain.

1:2

NASB, NJB, LXX
"mourns. . .dries up"

NKJV, Peshitta
"mourn. . .withers"

NRSV
"wither. . .dries up"

REB
"dried up. . .parched"

TEV
"dry up. . .turn brown"

JPSOA
"languish. . .wither"

NET
"bellowing. . .wilt"

The first VERB (BDB 5, KB 6, Qal PERFECT with waw)
seems to parallel the second VERB (BDB 386, KB 384, Qal PERFECT with waw).
The problem is that the first VERB has such a large semantic field reflecting several different connotations
to the root (אבל). It could denote "withering" or "mourning." Both fit usages in Amos. I think they are parallel.

verses.zh: 耶和华如此说：大马士革三番四次地犯罪，我必不免去她的刑罚；因为她以打粮食的铁器打过基列。
verses.en: This is what the Lord says:“Because Damascus has committed three crimes[NOTE:1]—make that four![NOTE:2]—I will not revoke my decree of judgment.[NOTE:3] They ripped through Gilead like threshing sledges with iron teeth.[NOTE:4]
notes: Traditionally, “transgressions” or “sins.” The word refers to rebellion against authority and is used in the international political realm (see 1 Kgs 12:19; 2 Kgs 1:1; 3:5, 7; 8:22). There is debate over its significance in this context. Some relate the “rebellion” of the foreign nations to God’s mandate to Noah (Gen 9:5-7). This mandate is viewed as a treaty between God and humankind, whereby God holds humans accountable to populate the earth and respect his image as it is revealed in all people. While this option is a possible theological explanation of the message in light of the Old Testament as a whole, nothing in these oracles alludes to that Genesis passage. J. Barton suggests that the prophet is appealing to a common morality shared across the ancient Near East regarding the conduct of war, since all of the oracles can be related to activities and atrocities committed in warfare (Amos’s Oracles against the Nations [SOTSMS], 39-61). The “transgression” then would be a violation of what all cultures would take as fundamental human decency. Some argue that the nations cited in Amos 1-2 had been members of the Davidic empire. Their crime would consist of violating the mutual agreements that all should have exhibited toward one another (cf. M. E. Polley, Amos and the Davidic Empire). This interpretation is connected to the notion that Amos envisions a reconstituted Davidic empire for Israel and the world (9:11-15). Ultimately, we can only speculate what lay behind Amos’ thinking. He does not specify the theological foundation of his universal moral vision, but it is clear that Amos believes that all nations are responsible before the Lord for their cruelty toward other human beings. He also assumes that even those who did not know his God would recognize their inhumane treatment of others as inherently wrong. The translation “crimes” is general enough to communicate that a standard (whether human or divine) has been breached. For a survey of the possible historical events behind each oracle, see S. M. Paul, Amos (Hermeneia).

Heb “Because of three violations of Damascus, even because of four.”sn The three…four style introduces each of the judgment oracles of chaps. 1-2. Based on the use of a similar formula in wisdom literature (see Prov 30:18-19, 29-31), one expects to find in each case a list of four specific violations. However, only in the eighth oracle (against Israel) does one find the expected fourfold list. Through this adaptation and alteration of the normal pattern the Lord indicates that his focus is Israel (he is too bent on judging Israel to dwell very long on her neighbors) and he emphasizes Israel’s guilt with respect to the other nations. (Israel’s list fills up before the others’ lists do.) See R. B. Chisholm, “For Three Sins…Even for Four: The Numerical Sayings in Amos,” BSac 147 (1990): 188-97.

Heb “I will not bring it [or “him”] back.” The pronominal object seems to refer to the decree of judgment that follows; the referent (the decree) has been specified in the translation for clarity. See S. M. Paul, Amos (Hermeneia), 46-47. Another option is to understand the suffix as referring to the particular nation mentioned in the oracle and to translate, “I will not take him [i.e., that particular nation] back.” In this case the Lord makes it clear that he does not intend to resume treaty relations with the nation in view. See M. L. Barré, “The Meaning of lʾ ʾšybnw in Amos 1:3-2:6, ” JBL 105 (1986): 622.

Like threshing sledges with iron teeth. A threshing sledge was made of wooden boards embedded with sharp stones or iron teeth. As the sledge was pulled over the threshing floor, the stones or iron teeth would separate the grain from the stalks. See O. Borowski, Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 64-65. Here the threshing metaphor is used to emphasize how violently and inhumanely the Arameans (the people of Damascus) had treated the people of Gilead (located east of the Jordan River).tn Heb “they threshed [or “trampled down”] Gilead with sharp iron implements” (NASB similar).
verses.commentary:
1:3 "Thus says the Lord" This prophetic formula was a way of showing
that the message was not the personal opinion of the prophet, but the very word of God. How much of the
message was from the prophet (specific vocabulary, literary form) is uncertain. The mood or manner of inspiration
is uncertain and may have variations, but the important truth is that it is a message from God. This message,
though given in a certain language, historical situation, and culture, has a relevance to all cultures and times.
Hermeneutically every passage has one meaning—that which the original inspired author meant to say—but
many applications or significances related to the reader/hearer's historical and cultural situation. However, the
application must be directly related to the original author's intent/message!

In this context the phrase announces the judgment of YHWH on nations and peoples
(cf. Jer. 47:2; 48:1; Ezek. 25:3; 30:2; Amos 1:3; 2:1).

"Bible Interpretation Seminar"

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

▣ "For three transgressions of Damascus and for four" This is a standard introductory
phrase in Amos (cf. Amos 1:3,6,9,11,13; 2:1,4,6). It has also been found in other Near Eastern literature. It
means that they sinned again and again.

The term "four" was used often in the Ancient Near East.

- four phases of the moon

- four divisions of the year (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 495)

In the OT itself it represented

- compass directions (i.e. a man facing east)

- wind directions (e.g. Dan. 7:2; 8:8)

- corners of the earth (e.g. Isa. 11:12)

From these came its implied meaning of completeness or fullness. Also the numbers
three and four equals seven, which is another OT way to show completeness; the sins of these
nations were full/complete!

The term "transgressions" (BDB 833, KB 981) is one of several Hebrew words which are used
to describe sin and rebellion. In Amos this term takes on a sense of social sins (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 708).
These nations rebel by attacking neighbors and relatives. Their actions show that they do not know YHWH.
These nations were part of the Davidic empire and had been exposed to the worship of YHWH. These nations
will be a part of a restored Davidic kingdom (cf. Amos 9:11-15; see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)!

Prophets often spoke of YHWH's judgment on the nations (cf. Isa. 13-23; Jer. 46-51;
Ezek. 25-32).

▣ "Damascus" The nation of Syria is also known as Aram with Damascus as its capital. The capital
stands for the nation as a whole. It was besieged and captured by the Assyrian King Adad-Nirari III (796 B.C.),
according to Assyrian Annals.

▣

NASB, NRSV, JPSOA
"I will not revoke its punishment"

NKJV, Peshitta
"I will not turn away its punishment"

TEV
"I will certainly punish them"

NJB
"I have made my decree and will not

relent"

REB
"I will grant them no reprieve"

LXX
"I will not turn away from him"

The NEGATED VERB (BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil IMPERFECT)
is the usual VERB in the prophets to describe "repentance" (see SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE [OT]).
In this context the "I" refers to YHWH. The only vocabulary available to us to describe God relates to humans. God is an eternal Spirit.
We use human words to describe Him (anthropomorphisms), but He is far beyond our ability to describe. However, He is affected by
repentance and prayer (see SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS
OF HUMAN LANGUAGE)

The question remains, "What is 'it' (see vv. 9,11,13)"? In context, it seems to refer to a common sense
understanding of what is appropriate in human relations between nations.

- These surrounding nations had been under the influence of David and Solomon, therefore, they had some knowledge of YHWH's law.

- This refers to "natural revelation." See exegetical notes at Ps. 19:1-6 and also Rom. 1:18-23 (i.e. God known through nature); Rom. 2:14-15
(i.e. inner moral witness)

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

▣ "they threshed Gilead with implements of sharp iron" "They" refers to the Syrians.

The VERB (BDB 190, KB 218,Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)
refers to an agricultural procedure of separating grain from its husk (cf. Deut. 25:4; 2 Sam. 24:22; Isa. 28:28). It is used as imagery in
2 Kgs. 13:7; Isa. 21:10; Jer. 50:11; and Hosea 10:11. It is used of God's judgment (e.g. Micah 4:13 and Hab. 3:12).

Here it could also be imagery, but because of the Septuagint's translation of 2 Sam. 12:31, it may
be literal. Whether figurative or literal, it speaks of Syrian abuses of Israelites (possibly related to 2 Kgs. 13:1-9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

▣ "Gilead" This name (BDB 166) refers to the northern trans-jordan area between the
Arnon and Jabbok Rivers that was given to the sons of Jacob, Reuben, and Gad. The specific atrocities
of Syria (Aram) may relate to 2 Kgs. 8:28-29 or 10:32-33.

verses.zh: 我却要降火在哈薛的家中，烧灭便哈达的宫殿。
verses.en: So I will set Hazael’s house[NOTE:1] on fire;fire[NOTE:2] will consume Ben Hadad’s[NOTE:3] fortresses.
notes: “Hazael’s house” (“the house of Hazael”) refers to the dynasty of Hazael.sn Hazael took the throne of Aram in 843 b.c. and established a royal dynasty. See 2 Kgs 8:7-15 and W. Pitard, Ancient Damascus, 145-60.
Heb “it”; the referent (the fire mentioned in the previous line) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Ben Hadad may refer to Hazael’s son and successor (2 Kgs 13:3, 24) or to an earlier king (see 1 Kgs 20), perhaps the ruler whom Hazael assassinated when he assumed power.
verses.commentary:
1:4 "I will send fire" The VERB (BDB 1018, KB 1511, Piel PERFECT
with waw), is parallel to "consume," "break," and "cut off." YHWH will destroy the
fortifications and dynasty of the house of Hazael (Syria, Aram). Fire is a symbol of the judgment of God on
wickedness (e.g. Isa. 30:27; Jer. 21:14; Ezek. 20:47-48; Zeph. 1:18; 3:8; Mal. 4:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

▣ "Hazael" This was the usurper monarch of Syria (BDB 303, cf. 2 Kgs. 8:7-15). He reigned
from 843-796 B.C.(?). He was a powerful military adversary to Assyria's western expansion. Syria
was invaded several times, but Damascus was not taken (i.e. 841, 837, and possibly 836 B.C.).

Once Assyrian pressure was lessened Hazael attacked his southern neighbors.

- trans-Jordan area, 2 Kgs. 10:32-33

- Philistia, 2 Kgs. 12:17

- Judah, 2 Kgs. 12:17-18

This reference is anachronism to an earlier title for Syria/Aram (i.e. "the House of Hazael").

▣ "citadels" The term (BDB 74) is translated in various ways:

- stronghold

- guardroom of the palace or temple

- fortress

The Akkadian loanword, b'rh, is used as a parallel in the Post-Exilic literature
(e.g. of forts in 2 Chr. 17:12; 27:4 and of the temple in 1 Chr. 29:1; Neh. 2:8).

▣ "Ben-hadad" This (lit. "son of Hadad," BDB 122, cf. 2 Kgs. 13:3,24-25) is
the "son of Hazael" (i.e. he reigned from 797-775 B.C.?). Probably his father gave him this name (in history as
Ben Hadad III) because it became the common name (dynastic title) of many Syrian monarchs, like Pharaoh in Egypt or Caesar in Rome.

It is also possible that it reflects the worship of the storm god, Hadad (Ba'al or
Rimmon, cf. 2 Kgs. 5:18). In this case it would be a condemnation on idolatry.

verses.zh: 我必折断大马士革的门闩，剪除亚文平原的居民和伯•伊甸掌权的。亚兰人必被掳到吉珥。这是耶和华说的。
verses.en: I will break the bar on the gate[NOTE:1] of Damascus.I will remove[NOTE:2] the ruler[NOTE:3] from Wicked Valley,[NOTE:4] the one who holds the royal scepter from Beth Eden.[NOTE:5] The people of Aram will be deported to Kir.”[NOTE:6] The Lord has spoken!
notes: The bar on the city gate symbolizes the city’s defenses and security.
Heb “cut off.”

Heb “the one who sits.” Some English versions take the Hebrew term in a collective sense as “inhabitants” (e.g., KJV, NKJV, NASB, NRSV). The context and the parallel in the next clause (“the one who holds the royal scepter”), however, suggest that the royal house is in view. For this term (יוֹשֵׁב, yoshev), see N. K. Gottwald, The Tribes of Yahweh, 512-30.

Heb “valley of wickedness.” Though many English versions take the Hebrew phrase בִקְעַת־אָוֶן (biqʿat ʾaven) as a literal geographical place name (“Valley of Aven” in NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT), it appears to be a derogatory epithet for Damascus and the kingdom of Aram.
Many associate the name “Beth Eden” with Bit Adini, an Aramean state located near the Euphrates River, but it may be a sarcastic epithet meaning “house of pleasure.”
According to Amos 9:7, the Arameans originally came from Kir. The Lord threatens to reverse their history and send them back there.
verses.commentary:
1:5 "the gate bar of Damascus" Literally this refers to the lock on the main gate, a large
wooden beam (or sometimes a metal bar, cf. 1 Kgs. 4:13), which was placed horizontally across two
wooden doors. Symbolically, it refers to the destruction and exile of Syria (Aram) as a nation (cf. TEV).

▣

NASB, NKJV, NJB
"the inhabitant"

NRSV, TEV, Peshitta, JPSOA, LXX
"the inhabitants"

NIV
"the king"

NET
"the ruler"

JB
"the one enthroned"

This is a Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE MASCULINE SINGULAR
(BDB 442, KB 444, which means "to sit," "to dwell," or "to remain"). It is obvious there is a parallel between
this term and the SINGULAR "him."

- Amos 1:5c, "him who holds the scepter"

- Amos 1:8b, "him who holds the scepter"

The Rotherham's Emphasized Bible has in the footnote, "him that is seated = that reigneth"
(p. 873). Therefore, it seems that NIV, NET, JB have the contextual sense.

▣ "the Valley of Aven" The term "Aven" (BDB 20) can mean

- trouble

- sorrow

- wickedness

- idolatry

It is used in several ways in Amos-Hosea.

- a place of idolatry (here)

- a reference to Bethel by means of a Hebrew word play (cf. Hosea 4:15; 5:8; 10:5,8)

- a reference to wickedness (cf. Hosea 6:8; 10:8; 12:11)

- nothingness (i.e. idolatry as vanity, cf. Amos 5:5)

Here, it refers to a place somewhere in Syria. The Expositor's Bible Commentary,
vol. 7, p. 284, notes that it is a Jewish word play on the city of Baalbek, which was called Heliopolis during the
Greek period. McComiskey also asserts that because of the contact between Syria and Egypt this city
may possibly have taken on the name of an Egyptian city, 'On (i.e. BDB 58 and the Septuagint, cf.
Gen. 41:50; Exod. 30:17 and the Oxford NRSV Annotated Bible, p. 1171).

The site is geographically uncertain, but many believe that it refers to the Beqaa or Bekaa valley of Syria (i.e. the Septuagint).

▣ "him who holds the scepter" Originally the term "scepter" (BDB 986) referred to a
wooden implement of war. Leaders were those who fought well. Here it refers to the Syrian king.

Their wooden weapon became a symbol of authority, rule, or power. It is used of

- the kings of pagan nations in Isa. 14:5; Amos 1:5,8; Zech. 10:11

- God's power in Isa. 10:5

- His Messiah's power in Isa. 11:4

▣ "Beth-eden" This name means "house of pleasure" (BDB 108 CONSTRUCT BDB 112). Its
geographical location is uncertain, but may refer to

- a kingdom north of Aram on the bank of the Euphrates River in the time of Assurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III

- Baalbek in the Bukaa Valley in the time of Tiglath-pileser III

- simply sarcasm

▣ "So the people of Syria will be exiled to Kir" We learn from Amos 9:7 that this was their original
homeland; they will be exiled to where they started from (BDB 885, cf. 2 Kgs. 16:9). However, its location
is unknown. Most identify it as a location in Elam (cf. Isa. 22:6), but also possibly a region in northern Aram.

verses.zh: 耶和华如此说：迦萨三番四次地犯罪，我必不免去她的刑罚；因为她掳掠众民交给以东。
verses.en: This is what the Lord says:“Because Gaza[NOTE:1] has committed three crimes[NOTE:2]—make that four![NOTE:3]—I will not revoke my decree of judgment.[NOTE:4] They deported a whole community[NOTE:5] and sold them[NOTE:6] to Edom.
notes: Gaza was one of the five major Philistine cities (along with Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, and Gath). It was considered to mark the southern limit of Canaan at the point on the coast where it was located (Gen 10:19).

Traditionally, “transgressions” (KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV) or “sins” (NIV). For an explanation of the atrocities outlined in this oracle as treaty violations of God’s mandate to Noah in Gen 9:5-7, see the note on the word “violations” in 1:3.
Heb “Because of three violations of Gaza, even because of four.”sn On the three…four style that introduces each of the judgment oracles of chaps. 1-2 see the note on the word “four” in 1:3.

Heb “I will not bring it [or “him”] back.” The translation understands the pronominal object to refer to the decree of judgment that follows; the referent (the decree) has been specified in the translation for clarity. For another option see the note on the word “judgment” in 1:3.
Heb “[group of] exiles.” A number of English translations take this as a collective singular and translate it with a plural (e.g., NAB, NIV, NRSV).
Heb “in order to hand them over.”
verses.commentary:
1:6 "Gaza" This city (BDB 738) was a way of referring to the nation of Philistia. They were sea
peoples from the Aegean Islands who tried to invade Egypt, but were defeated and settled on the
southwestern coast of Palestine around 1200 B.C. They brought Iron Age technology
with them and established control over a large area of the coastland. In Amos 1:6-8 four of their five
major city-states are mentioned, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, and Gaza (cf. Zeph. 2:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PHILISTINES

▣ "because they deported an entire population" Apparently the descendants of Esau were
actively involved in purchasing Hebrew slaves taken by the Philistines (i.e. Ezek. 27:13). Entire communities
were captured and sold (cf. Joel 3:3-8 and possibly 2 Chr. 21:16-17).

▣ "Edom" Edom, Moab, and Ammon were relatives of the Israelites. They lived in the southern trans-Jordan.

The JPSOA suggests an emendation to "Aram," both here and in v. 9. Aram would denote Syria (i.e. Isa. 9:11).

- Edom ‒ אדם

- Aram ‒ ארם

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDOM AND ISRAEL

verses.zh: 我却要降火在迦萨的城内，烧灭其中的宫殿。
verses.en: So I will set Gaza’s city wall[NOTE:1] on fire;fire[NOTE:2] will consume her fortresses.
notes: The city wall symbolizes the city’s defenses and security.
Heb “it”; the referent (the fire mentioned in the previous line) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 我必剪除亚实突的居民和亚实基伦掌权的，也必反手攻击以革伦。非利士人所余剩的必都灭亡。这是主耶和华说的。
verses.en: I will remove[NOTE:1] the ruler[NOTE:2] from Ashdod,[NOTE:3] the one who holds the royal scepter from Ashkelon.[NOTE:4] I will strike Ekron[NOTE:5] with my hand;[NOTE:6] the rest of the Philistines will also die.”[NOTE:7] The Sovereign Lord has spoken!
notes: Heb “cut off.”
Heb “the one who sits.” Some translations take this expression as a collective singular referring to the inhabitants rather than the ruler (e.g., NAB, NRSV, NLT).
Ashdod was one of the five major Philistine cities (along with Ashkelon, Ekron, Gaza, and Gath).
Ashkelon was one of the five major Philistine cities (along with Ashdod, Ekron, Gaza, and Gath).
Ekron was one of the five major Philistine cities (along with Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gaza, and Gath).
Heb “I will turn my hand against Ekron.” For other uses of the idiom “turn the hand against,” see Ps 81:14; Isa 1:25; Jer 6:9; Zech 13:7.

Heb “and the remnant of the Philistines will perish.” The translation above assumes that reference is made to other Philistines beside those living in the cities mentioned. Another option is to translate, “Every last Philistine will die.”
verses.commentary:
1:8 "him who holds the scepter" David Allan Hubbard, "Joel and Amos," Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries,
pp. 133 and 136), makes the historical point that Amos is accurate regarding:

- the Philistine cities were royal city-states surrounded by other cities ruled by those who
bore the scepter of the city-state monarch (Amos 1:7)

- the Ammonites had a monarch and his officials (cf. Amos 1:15; Hosea 7:3,5,7,16; 8:4; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: AMMON)

▣ "the remnant of the Philistines will perish" The Philistines (BDB 814) were a traditional
enemy of Judah from the time of Joshua to David. They will be completely destroyed as a nation and as a people.

▣ "My power" This is literally "I will turn My hand. . ." The VERB "turn" (BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil
PERFECT) has a wide semantic field. It is used often of repentance toward God or turning away from God. Here,
it denotes God turning in judgment.

The term "hand" is imagery for power/action (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND).
This particular phrasing is also used in Ps. 81:14; Isa. 1:25; Ezek. 38:12; Zech. 13:7.

Another common phrase is "to stretch our your hand/arm" (i.e. Jer. 6:12; 15:6; Ezek. 6:14; 14:9,13; 16:27;
20:33; 25:7,13,16; 35:3).

▣ "the Lord God" This is literally Adon YHWH. Since
both are translated "lord," when they occur together YHWH is translated all capitals "God."
The title is very common in Amos.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

verses.zh: 耶和华如此说：泰尔三番四次地犯罪，我必不免去她的刑罚；因为她将众民交给以东，并不记念弟兄的盟约。
verses.en: This is what the Lord says:“Because Tyre has committed three crimes[NOTE:1]—make that four[NOTE:2]—I will not revoke my decree of judgment.[NOTE:3] They sold[NOTE:4] a whole community[NOTE:5] to Edom;they failed to observe[NOTE:6] a treaty of brotherhood.[NOTE:7]
notes: Traditionally, “transgressions” (KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV) or “sins” (NIV). For an explanation of the atrocities outlined in this oracle as treaty violations of God’s mandate to Noah in Gen 9:5-7, see the note on the word “violations” in 1:3.
Heb “Because of three violations of Tyre, even because of four.”sn On the three…four style that introduces each of the judgment oracles of chaps. 1-2 see the note on the word “four” in 1:3.

Heb “I will not bring it [or “him”] back.” The translation understands the pronominal object to refer to the decree of judgment that follows; the referent (the decree) has been specified in the translation for clarity. For another option see the note on the word “judgment” in 1:3.
Heb “handed over.”
Heb “[group of] exiles.” A similar phrase occurs in v. 6.
Heb “did not remember.”

A treaty of brotherhood. In the ancient Near-Eastern world familial terms were sometimes used to describe treaty partners. In a treaty between superior and inferior parties, the lord would be called “father” and the subject “son.” The partners in a treaty between equals referred to themselves as “brothers.” For biblical examples, see 1 Kgs 9:13 and 20:32-33.
verses.commentary:
1:9 "Tyre" This (BDB 862) refers to the nation of Phoenicia, which seems to have been
made up racially of Canaanites and the Sea Peoples (Aegean Sea). This nation became the source
of the fertility worship of both Ba'al and Asherah, which permeated the Northern Ten Tribes through
the influence of Jezebel (cf. 1 Kgs. 16:31-33; 18:19,21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "I will not revoke its punishment" This parallels vv. 3,11,13. See note at v. 3.

▣ "because they delivered up an entire population to Edom" Homer mentions Tyre's
slave trade in his Odyssey 4:288ff; 15:473ff.

▣ "did not remember the covenant of brotherhood" This refers to some type of treaty, possibly
the precedent of one that was made with Solomon (cf. 2 Sam. 5: 11; 1 Kgs. 5:1-18; 9: 11- 14). It also may
refer to the unnatural behavior of selling one's neighbor (i.e. blood relative) into slavery. All of the sins mentioned in this section
deal with mankind's inhumanity toward his fellowman. Phoenicia not only violated YHWH's laws, it violated the common mores of the ANE.

verses.zh: 我却要降火在泰尔的城内，烧灭其中的宫殿。
verses.en: So I will set fire to Tyre’s city wall;[NOTE:1] fire[NOTE:2] will consume her fortresses.”
notes: The city wall symbolizes the city’s defenses and security.
Heb “it”; the referent (the fire mentioned in the previous line) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
1:10 "I will send fire upon the wall of Tyre,

And it will consume her citadels" Tyre (capital of
Phoenicia) was an island fortress that was almost impregnable. However, during Alexander the Great's
move through Palestine in 332 B.C., after a seven-month siege, the city
fell when the enemy built a causeway out of the rubble of the destroyed mainland city. We learn from
historical documents that 6,000 were killed, 2,000 were crucified or impaled and 30,000 were sold into slavery.

Nebuchadnezzar II never took the island citadel, but after many years, it surrendered by treaty.

verses.zh: 耶和华如此说：以东三番四次地犯罪，我必不免去她的刑罚；因为她拿刀追赶兄弟，毫无怜悯，发怒撕裂，永怀忿怒。
verses.en: This is what the Lord says:“Because Edom has committed three crimes[NOTE:1]—make that four[NOTE:2]—I will not revoke my decree of judgment.[NOTE:3] He chased his brother[NOTE:4] with a sword;he wiped out his allies.[NOTE:5] In his anger he tore them apart without stopping to rest;[NOTE:6] in his fury he relentlessly attacked them.[NOTE:7]
notes: Traditionally, “transgressions” (KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV) or “sins” (NIV). For an explanation of the atrocities outlined in this oracle as treaty violations of God’s mandate to Noah in Gen 9:5-7, see the note on the word “violations” in 1:3.
Heb “Because of three violations of Edom, even because of four.”sn On the three…four style that introduces each of the judgment oracles of chaps. 1-2 see the note on the word “four” in 1:3.

Heb “I will not bring it [or “him”] back.” The translation understands the pronominal object to refer to the decree of judgment that follows; the referent (the decree) has been specified in the translation for clarity. For another option see the note on the word “judgment” in 1:3.

It is likely that “brother” refers here to a treaty partner (see the note on the word “brotherhood” in 1:9). However, it is possible, if Israel is in view, that Edom’s ancient blood relationship to God’s people is alluded to here. Cf. NCV, NLT “their relatives, the Israelites.”

Or “He stifled his compassion.” The Hebrew term רָחֲמָיו (rakhamayv) is better understood here (parallel to “brother/treaty partner”) as a reference to “allies” that Edom betrayed. An Aramaic cognate is attested (see DNWSI 2:1069-70). See M. Fishbane, “The Treaty Background of Amos 1:11 and Related Matters,” JBL 89 (1970): 313-18; idem, “Critical Note: Additional Remarks on rḥmyw (Amos 1:11),” JBL 91 (1972): 391-93; and M. Barré, “Amos 1:11 reconsidered,” CBQ 47 (1985) 420-27. Some argue that the clause is best translated as “and destroyed his womenfolk.” רַחַם (rakham) means “womb”; the plural here would be a metonymy for “women” and could establish a parallel with the atrocity of 1:13. See S. M. Paul, Amos (Hermeneia), 64-65.
Heb “his anger tore continually.” The Hebrew verb טָרַף (taraf, “tear apart”) is often used of an animal tearing apart its prey. The word picture here is that of a vicious predator’s feeding frenzy.

Traditionally, “he kept his fury continually.” The Hebrew term שְׁמָרָה (shemarah) could be taken as a Qal perfect third person masculine singular with third person feminine singular suffix (with mappiq omitted), “he kept it” (NASB, NKJV, NRSV). It is also possible in light of the parallelism that שָׁמַר (shamar) is a rare homonym cognate to an Akkadian verb meaning “to rage; to be furious.” Repointing the verb as שָׁמְרָה (shamerah, third person feminine singular), one could translate literally, “his fury raged continually” (NIV, NJPS).
verses.commentary:
1:11 "Edom" This (BDB 10) refers to near relatives of the Israelites through Esau,
Gen. 25:19-26; 36:1-19. Edom and Israel were always at odds. Edom becomes a symbol of broken
family bonds and covenants. She is often condemned in the prophets (cf. Isa. 34:5-17; 63:1-6;
Jer. 49:7-22; Lam. 4:21-22; Ezek. 25:12-14; 35:1-15; Mal. 1:2-4).

Petra was its capital (cf. Ps. 137:7; Ezek. 25:12-14; Obad. vv. 10-15; Mal. 1:2-4). It was
located east of Judah in the trans-Jordan region (modern Jordan).

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDOM AND ISRAEL

▣ "I will not revoke its. . ." This is a parallel phrase with no stated object, vv. 3,8,11. See note at v. 3.

▣

NASB
"compassion"

NKJV, NRSV, NJB, JPSOA, Peshitta
"pity"

TEV
"mercy"

REB
"natural affections"

This term (BDB 933) can also refer to a treaty partner (i.e. "ally," NIV footnote and NET Bible), thereby
parallel to "brother" in line d.

The LXX follows a different ancient Hebrew text, "and he spoiled a womb upon the ground and seized his
shivering fight for a testimony."

▣ "His anger also tore continually,

And he maintained his fury forever"

These two poetic lines are parallel. "His anger" refers to the settled, continual anger of the
Edomites against the Israelis. The PRONOUNS in this verse are ambiguous. They refer to two
different subjects.

- YHWH ‒ line c

- Edom/Aram ‒ line b, d-e

- Lines f, g could refer to either one, but the parallelism seems to prefer #2 in the last two poetic lines.

Again, God's judgment comes because of sins against people, in this case relatives (option #1 above).

The VERB "tore" (BDB 382, KB 380, Qal IMPERFECT) is used of
lions tearing apart their prey (i.e. Ps. 7:2; Ezek. 22:25). Notice YHWH is characterized as a lion in v. 2. Here, Edom's sins
against humanity are characterized with the same violent VERB.

The JPSOA on the last line of poetry in v. 11 has, "And his fury stormed unchecked." This is an emendation
from the MT.

- MT ‒ שׁמר, denoting "guard" (BDB 1036, KB 1581)

- Akkadian root ‒ שמר, denoting "anger," thereby a better poetic parallel to line 4

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER, PERPETUITY (BDB 664, KB 773)

verses.zh: 我却要降火在提幔，烧灭波斯拉的宫殿。
verses.en: So I will set Teman[NOTE:1] on fire;fire[NOTE:2] will consume Bozrah’s[NOTE:3] fortresses.”
notes: Teman was an important region (or perhaps city) in Edom.
Heb “it”; the referent (the fire mentioned in the previous line) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Bozrah was a city located in northern Edom.
verses.commentary:
1:12 "Teman" This (BDB 412) was a northern district of Edom (cf. Jer. 49:7,20; Obad. 9) whose capital was Bozrah.

▣ "Bozrah" This (BDB 131) refers to one of the larger northern cities of Edom located at a
major oasis on "the King's Highway" (trans-Jordan trade route from the Gulf of Aqaba north to Damascus). It was a
city of great antiquity (cf. Gen. 36:33; 1 Chr. 1:44). It will be destroyed by YHWH (cf. Jer. 49:13).

verses.zh: 耶和华如此说：亚扪人三番四次地犯罪，我必不免去他们的刑罚；因为他们剖开基列的孕妇，扩张自己的境界。
verses.en: This is what the Lord says:“Because the Ammonites have committed three crimes[NOTE:1]—make that four[NOTE:2]—I will not revoke my decree of judgment.[NOTE:3] They ripped open Gilead’s pregnant women[NOTE:4] so they could expand their territory.
notes: Traditionally, “transgressions” (KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV) or “sins” (NIV). For an explanation of the atrocities outlined in this oracle as treaty violations of God’s mandate to Noah in Gen 9:5-7, see the note on the word “violations” in 1:3.
Heb “Because of three violations of the Ammonites, even because of four.” On the three…four style that introduces each of the judgment oracles of chaps. 1-2 see the note on the word “four” in 1:3.

Heb “I will not bring it [or “him”] back.” The translation understands the pronominal object to refer to the decree of judgment that follows; the referent (the decree) has been specified in the translation for clarity. For another option see the note on the word “judgment” in 1:3.

The Ammonites ripped open Gilead’s pregnant women in conjunction with a military invasion designed to expand their territory. Such atrocities, although repugnant, were not uncommon in ancient Near Eastern warfare.
verses.commentary:
1:13 "Ammon" This (BDB 769) is also a relative of the Israelis through Lot (cf. Gen. 19:30-38). The
Israelites were not to confront them on their exodus because they were relatives (cf. Deut. 2:19). Ammon
was located in the trans-jordan area between the Arnon and Jabbok Rivers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMMON

▣ "Because they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead" Gilead (BDB 166) is in the
northern trans-jordan area. There is no historical reference to this specific act, but this practice was
well known (cf. 2 Kgs. 8:12; 15:16; Hosea 13:16). However, the judgment of YHWH falls on all of these
nations because of their violent war practices.

The NET Bible, p. 1590, # 11, suggests that "brother" (BDB 26) in v. 11, comes from the word "womb"
and, therefore, may refer to the slaughter of women (cf. LXX of v. 11). If so, verse 13 is a parallel of the horrible acts of
these other ANE nations.

▣ "In order to enlarge their borders" This slaughter of innocent women and children was
not related to holy war, as was the Israeli attack on Jericho (cf. Joshua 6), but was simply motivated by greed for more land.

verses.zh: 我却要在争战呐喊的日子，旋风狂暴的时候，点火在拉巴的城内，烧灭其中的宫殿。
verses.en: So I will set fire to Rabbah’s[NOTE:1] city wall;[NOTE:2] fire[NOTE:3] will consume her fortresses.War cries will be heard on the day of battle;[NOTE:4] a strong gale will blow on the day of the windstorm.[NOTE:5]
notes: Rabbah was the Ammonite capital.
The city wall symbolizes the city’s defenses and security.
Heb “it”; the referent (the fire mentioned in the previous line) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “with a war cry in the day of battle.”
Heb “with wind in the day of the windstorm.”sn A windstorm is a metaphor for judgment and destruction in the OT (see Isa 29:6; Jer 23:19) and ancient Near Eastern literature.
verses.commentary:
1:14 "Rabbah" This term means "the great" (BDB 913). This title was used of a city of Ammon, located at
the headwaters of the Jabbok River (cf. Deut. 3:11; 2 Sam. 12:26; 17:27), which served as the captial of Ammon.

▣

NASB, NJB, REB
"war cries"

NKJV, NRSV, TEV, JPSOA, Peshitta
"shouting"

LXX
"a cry on the day of battle"

This term (BDB 929) has a large semantical field:

- raise a shout

- for attack

- for victory

- for worship

- for destruction

- give a blast

Often a battle cry is linked to a trumpet blast, as in Josh. 6:5,10,16,20. Every nation had
its own war cry (cf. Amos 2:2; 1 Sam. 17:20,52, also see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 1, pp. 9,254).
Israel's was linked to YHWH (cf. Jdg. 7:20-21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORNS USED BY ISRAEL

verses.zh: 他们的王和首领必一同被掳去。这是耶和华说的。
verses.en: Ammon’s[NOTE:1] king will be deported;[NOTE:2] he and his officials[NOTE:3] will be carried off[NOTE:4] together.”The Lord has spoken!
notes: Heb “their”; the referent (Ammon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “will go into exile.”
Or “princes” (KJV, NAB, NASB, NLT); cf. TEV “officers,” CEV “leaders.”
The words “will be carried off” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

* Although they are not inspired, paragraph divisions are the key to understanding and following the original author's intent. Each modern translation
has divided and summarized the paragraphs. Every paragraph has one central topic, truth, or thought. Each version encapsulates that topic in its own distinct way.
As you read the text, ask yourself which translation fits your understanding of the subject and verse divisions.

In every chapter we must read the Bible first and try to identify its subjects (paragraphs), then compare our understanding with the modern versions.
Only when we understand the original author's intent by following his logic and presentation can we truly understand the Bible. Only the original author is inspired-readers
have no right to change or modify the message. Bible readers do have the responsibility of applying the inspired truth to their day and their lives.

Note that all technical terms and abbreviations are explained fully in the following SPECIAL TOPICS:
Hebrew Grammatical Terms, Textual Criticism, and Glossary.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Chapters one and two form a literary unit dealing with the sins of the nations and of YHWH's covenant
people. The first two verses could be the theme of the entire book. Israel's (i.e. the
Northern Ten Tribes) unique relationship with YHWH causes them to be uniquely guilty of rebellion
(cf. Rom. 9:4-5). They were Covenant People and they had a Covenant assignment.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

- Amos begins his Sermon with judgment on the enemies of Israel:

- all the surrounding nations

- pagans

- those related to the Jews

(1) Edom by Esau

(2) Ammon, Moab by Lot

- her kinsmen, Judea

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: AMOS 1:1-2

1The words of Amos, who was among the sheepherders from Tekoa,
which he envisioned in visions concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.

2He said,

"The Lord roars from Zion

And from Jerusalem He utters His voice;

And the shepherds' pasture grounds mourn,

And the summit of Carmel dries up."
